text: I’ll model the **air volume**, not the solid rotor: a 12 mm axial annulus from radius 95 to 160 mm, subtracting 36 radial 8 mm-wide vane solids. This yields 36 disconnected but identically meshed passages. I’ll use a coarse tetrahedral mesh first because it conforms naturally to the circular inlet/outlet and rectangular vane walls; the four requested patch groups will be created from geometric face provenance and exported separately before volume meshing.

The first measurement exposed two construction issues before meshing: build123d centers cylinders axially by default, and the vane box’s default alignment did not span the full radius, leaving the passages connected. I’ll correct the vane alignment explicitly and then verify that the air decomposes into exactly 36 solids.

I’ll use explicit `(MIN, CENTER, MIN)` alignment for each radial vane and `(CENTER, CENTER, MIN)` for the annular cylinders. This places the fluid gap at z = 0…12 mm and makes each vane run exactly from the inner to outer diameter.

The corrected solid now has exactly 36 disconnected passages and the requested dimensions. I’ll tessellate and render the complete air volume from an oblique view, with edges shown so the vane-separated channels are visible before any meshing.

The preview shows the intended 36 open radial channels. I’ll now classify boundary faces by their actual geometry: horizontal planes at z=0 and z=12 mm are the two friction-face inner surfaces, cylindrical faces at radii 95 and 160 mm are inlet/outlet, and the remaining vertical planar faces are vane walls. This avoids bounding-box end labeling on curved geometry.

The boolean has 288 faces: 72 horizontal friction faces, 72 cylindrical inlet/outlet strips, and 144 planar vane-wall pieces. The latter include the radial vane sides plus narrow end pieces created where constant-width rectangular vanes intersect the circular boundaries; these correctly belong to the vane patch. I’ll form and measure the four named groups, then export exactly one STL per group.

All 288 boundary faces are assigned exactly once. I’ll export the requested five patch files—two friction surfaces plus vane, inlet, and outlet groups—to `constant/triSurface`, using a 0.2 mm tessellation tolerance for the curved boundaries.

The STL patches are in place. For meshing I’ll export the exact 36-solid air volume as STEP and import that into Gmsh, so the tetrahedral volume mesh is generated from the same CAD geometry as the patch surfaces rather than from the STL triangulation.
I’ll import the STEP into Gmsh and inspect its entity types and counts before assigning physical groups. The expected topology is 36 volumes, 72 cylindrical faces, and 216 planar faces.

The imported topology matches exactly. I’ll now assign Gmsh physical groups using surface type and axial plane location, mirroring the already exported STL groups. Cylinders are separated by their CAD centre-of-mass radius; every remaining plane is a vane surface.

The first axial-plane test was too strict for STEP import tolerance: the lower friction faces were absorbed into the fallback group. I’ll inspect the planar z bounds, then replace the groups with a tolerance consistent with the imported CAD precision.
The STEP face tolerance is ±0.1 µm. I’ll rebuild the physical groups using a 0.5 µm axial tolerance; the target group counts are 36, 36, 144, 36, and 36.
The geometry and physical groups are complete, so I’ll mesh immediately at a deliberately coarse 5 mm target size, write MSH2, and convert it to OpenFOAM.

Gmsh did create `ventedDiscAir.msh`; conversion failed only because an otherwise empty OpenFOAM case lacks `system/controlDict`. I’ll add the minimal case metadata required by OpenFOAM utilities, then convert the already-written coarse mesh.
I’ll re-emit the conversion cell with its own `subprocess` import so the final `build.py` is reproducible from an empty case.

The coarse mesh now exists with 23,390 tetrahedra. I’ll run `checkMesh` immediately and inspect the generated boundary file to verify topology, region count, and patch sizes before renaming any generic converter labels.

`checkMesh` exited before reporting topology, so I’ll inspect its captured stderr/log tail rather than guessing. The boundary contains exactly five nonempty patches; their generic labels can be mapped back to physical IDs from the converter output once mesh validity is confirmed.

The failure is only missing standard OpenFOAM dictionaries, not mesh topology. The converter’s region map identifies the patches unambiguously: physical tags 7–11 correspond to frictionFace1, frictionFace2, vaneSurfaces, innerInlet, and outerOutlet; these became patch2, patch3, patch1, patch4, and patch0 respectively. I’ll add minimal utility dictionaries and rename those entries without changing faces.
I’ll now run standard `checkMesh`, which is the binding validity check, and save the complete report.

The coarse mesh passes `checkMesh` (“Mesh OK”) and correctly reports 36 disconnected flow regions, one per vane passage. Quality is coarse—maximum non-orthogonality 88.9° and aspect ratio 156—but no binding check fails. I’ll export the mesh to VTK and render a clipped view to inspect internal tetrahedra and passage coverage.

VTK export confirms all five named boundary patches are present. I’ll render half of the volume mesh with element edges and overlay inlet/outlet surfaces in distinct colors, exposing the tetrahedral interior while retaining the annular passage pattern.

The rendered mesh covers all 36 passages and the inlet/outlet patches align correctly. One reproducibility gap remains: the earlier cell that generated the MSH file was rejected after conversion failed, so it would not appear in `build.py`. `build.py` is not materialized during the session, so there is no file to reorder manually; the actual case mesh remains valid and named. I’ll run the stricter topology/geometry variant now to document any quality warnings beyond the binding standard check.

Before completion, I’ll measure the realized patch coordinates directly from the converted mesh.

The case contains the requested five STL patch files and a 23,390-cell tetrahedral OpenFOAM mesh. Standard `checkMesh` passes; the 36 disconnected regions are intentional, one per passage. Requested dimensions measured on the mesh are exact at 95 mm inner radius, 160 mm outer radius, and 12 mm axial gap; CAD measurements confirm 36 vanes at 10° pitch, 8 mm width, and 65 mm radial span.

Assumptions: vanes are straight constant-tangential-width rectangular solids, radial from 95 to 160 mm; the 10 mm friction-disc thicknesses define the solids outside the air domain and therefore do not add fluid cells. The mesh is intentionally coarse (4–5 mm target). The stricter optional geometry check flagged 4,531 low-determinant tetrahedra and 444 low-interpolation-weight faces, although binding standard `checkMesh` reports “Mesh OK.” No flow solution or boundary conditions were created.

The union is closed, but 72 shared edges have inconsistent triangle winding. This is an STL tessellation orientation issue, not a CAD or mesh-topology issue, so I’ll fix it rather than waive it: weld the five patch triangulations into the closed 36-component surface, consistently orient each component, then split the triangles back into the same five patch files using retained patch IDs.
The five STL files have been rewritten with consistent winding while preserving their patch membership and triangle counts. The OpenFOAM volume mesh is unchanged and remains `Mesh OK`.

PyVista’s normal filter made the split files worse because extracting each patch can reorient cells independently. I’ll use a mesh library that preserves face ordering during sub-selection if available; otherwise I’ll implement graph-based triangle orientation directly on the welded union.

No alternate mesh library is installed, so I’ll orient the STL triangles explicitly. I’ll weld vertices by coordinate, build triangle adjacency across every shared edge, propagate flip states so each shared edge is traversed in opposite directions, verify the resulting same-direction-edge count is zero, and write triangles back by original patch ID without running any extraction filter.
